A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiNa-LRM research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original preference-prediction experiments, architectural and noise-schedule ablations, uncertainty measurements, and ReFL and Flow-GRPO alignment results.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds SDXL comparisons, reward-head ablations and an SD3.5-M-to-SD3.5-L reward-transfer experiment.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same noise-calibrated Thurstone formulation, fidelity loss, FiLM-conditioned gated Q-Former and multi-noise token ensembling. Additional backbone evaluations and alternative-head ablations do not revise the proposed default method.

E1.justification: Both versions use HPDv3 training data, the same four preference benchmarks and text-to-image alignment using Pick-a-Pic. Added SDXL and SD3.5-L experiments change model configurations within this coverage. Video, editing and audio-visual applications are discussed only as future extensions.

E2.justification: The main Table 1 comparator roster is unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates LRM-SDXL as an alignment comparator in Figure 5, whereas v1 compared it only on offline preference accuracy. Table 6 also introduces average-pooling and transformer-plus-pooling alternatives for the reward-head comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds a controlled SDXL ReFL comparison holding the generator and optimization configuration fixed while changing rewards, and an experiment transferring an SD3.5-M reward to SD3.5-L. These new alignment curves extend through 200 steps, alongside new head configurations. This substantially expands the evaluation design; the original 150-step SD3.5-M experiment and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds direct tests of reward-head aggregation, performance against LRM-SDXL with a matched backbone, and reuse of trained rewards across generators sharing a latent space. These address architectural dependence, backbone confounding and transferability. Earlier noise, layer-depth, uncertainty, Flow-GRPO and reward-hacking analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A retains the same 1,000 HPDv3 pairs, ten noise draws per pair, variation ratios, mean margins and score variances. The added experiments introduce no new seed reporting, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 newly reports 71.55% average accuracy for DiNa-LRM on SDXL against 61.73% for LRM-SDXL (Table 5). Table 6 adds pooling-head averages of 71.03% and 71.14%, alongside the retained 71.49% Q-Former result. Figures 5–6 add SDXL alignment and SD3.5-L transfer findings. Original numerical results remain unchanged; these are additional results, not improvements to the original experimental runs.

T1.justification: The diffusion and flow-matching definitions, preference likelihoods, uncertainty calibration, loss, ensembling equations and appendix uncertainty formulas are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list and main conclusion retain the same claims about diffusion-native preference modeling, noise ensembling, competitive reward accuracy and efficient alignment. The new experiments supply additional support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C.3 explicitly distinguishes reuse of the formulation across backbones from transfer of trained rewards within compatible latent spaces. Appendix D.2 discusses requirements for untested broader applications. The conclusion removes the specific grid-artifact observation and instead references reward-hacking patterns already documented in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds limited implementation descriptions for the comparison heads: direct pooling versus a lightweight transformer followed by pooling. The core hyperparameter tables, training and inference algorithms, hardware disclosure and project URL are unchanged; detailed implementation information for the added experiments remains limited.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting broader application discussion, including Reward Forcing, UniC and AnyTalker, plus a Visual-aware CoT citation in related work. The central positioning against algorithm-specific, step-level diffusion rewards remains unchanged. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes Appendix C into four subsections, expands Appendix D and adds acknowledgements and cross-references. Most existing prose remains intact. Some reference edits introduce errors, including 'Table 5.3' and 'Appendix 3' where v1 correctly referenced Section 5.3 and Table 3.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays with new SDXL and transfer plots (Figures 5–6), comparison and head-ablation tables (Tables 5–6), and an SDXL row in the backbone table. Existing figures and tables are retained but relocated or reformatted; v1 Figures 5–7 become v2 Figures 7–9.

improvement.justification: v1's comparison with prior diffusion rewards used different backbones. v2's matched-SDXL accuracy and alignment comparisons substantially reduce this important confounding, while head ablations and shared-latent-space transfer provide direct evidence for architectural robustness and reward reuse. These additions materially strengthen the central empirical case and clarify its limits. Sparse implementation details for the new experiments and minor cross-reference errors temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.
